The phrase "my compounds are on top of each other" is a common colloquialism in organic chemistry labs. It typically refers to thin-layer chromatography (TLC), where compounds are spotted on a plate and separated by polarity. If two compounds have very similar polarities, they will travel the same distance up the plate, causing their spots to overlap (i.e., be "on top of each other"). This means the chemist is struggling to separate them.

- (A) Similar boiling points would cause problems in distillation, but chemists would say "they co-distill" or "their boiling points are too close."
- (B) Similar optical rotations would not cause compounds to overlap physically or on a separation device; this is irrelevant to the phrase.
- (C) Non-covalent interactions (like π-stacking) could be described as "stacking," but in the context of a failed separation, "on top of each other" idiomatically refers to co-elution, not intermolecular bonding.

Answer: D
